title: New view of the Pillars of Creation: visible
caption: The Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Eagle Nebula, M 16, Messier 16 · constellation Serpens Cauda · about 7000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA/Hubble and the Hubble Heritage Team

recognition.text: Ranked #4 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Rust-colored columns rise through a multi-colored glow of gas, threaded with wispy tendrils of dark dust. These are the Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula, returning in a fresh visible-light portrait from the Hubble Space Telescope, which revisited one of its most famous and popular images.

The pillars are clouds of gas and dust, the kind of material from which new stars form. They are under constant attack. Intense radiation from young stars scorches their surfaces, and strong winds from massive stars nearby wear them away.

That is what makes a second look so valuable. The new images bring better contrast and a clearer view than before, letting astronomers track how the pillars' shape shifts over the years. Comparing views taken years apart turns a single snapshot into something closer to a time-lapse of a nebula being slowly eroded.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (4.53 x 4.72 arcminutes) and distance (7000 light years), the frame spans roughly 9.2 × 9.6 light-years. Its light set out about 7,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This view comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in visible light, using filters that isolate the glow of oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Each filter isolates one narrow band of light from a single element, so the colors are a scientific mapping, not the mix an eye would see, and the long exposures record gas far too faint to see directly.
